### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain.”

German

“Mit der Dummheit kämpfen Götter selbst vergebens.”

Literally “Against stupidity the gods themselves struggle in vain.” English usually softens kämpfen to “contend.”

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain.”
-   “Against stupidity even the gods struggle in vain.”

### Attribution notes

Schiller, Die Jungfrau von Orleans (The Maid of Orleans), Act III, Scene 6 — spoken by Talbot, not by Joan. Crediting it as a free-floating Schiller aphorism drops the dramatic speaker and the military defeat that prompts the line.

#### About Friedrich Schiller

Friedrich Schiller (1759–1805) linked aesthetics and freedom in Letters on the Aesthetic Education of Man, alongside major dramatic works.

### Interpretation

Schiller's line is usually read as resignation, but the mechanism is worth stating: stupidity here means not low intelligence but an inability to follow an argument one is being shown. Where a person will not or cannot track reasons, there is nothing for a better reason to engage, so the conflict is not one that argument can win. The gods are invoked precisely to make the point that even overwhelming power meets the same limit.

#### Why it matters

It clarifies a common frustration: explaining harder to someone who is not tracking the explanation wastes effort. The useful move is to find out whether the disagreement is about reasons at all.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain.”?

“Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain.” comes from The Maid of Orleans, attributed to Friedrich Schiller.

#### What does Friedrich Schiller mean by limits?

Across 4 recurring voices here (notably Ludwig Wittgenstein and John Stuart Mill), limits is framed through Analytic Philosophy and Utilitarianism. Some passages define limits; others warn how it fails; still others relocate it inside habit, community, or language. This passage enters that discussion through limits, critique.

#### Is the wording of this Friedrich Schiller quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain.” Forms in circulation that differ: Against stupidity the gods themselves contend in vain. / Against stupidity even the gods struggle in vain. The German reads “Mit der Dummheit kämpfen Götter selbst vergebens.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Schiller, Die Jungfrau von Orleans (The Maid of Orleans), Act III, Scene 6 — spoken by Talbot, not by Joan. Crediting it as a free-floating Schiller aphorism drops the dramatic speaker and the military defeat that prompts the line.
